name: Dry Tortugas National Park
author: author-D-2026-10-17
summary:
Almost 70 miles west of Key West, seven keys of coral reef and sand — the Dry Tortugas — lie within roughly 101 square miles of shoals and open water at the far end of the Florida Keys. Ponce de León named them Las Tortugas, the turtles, in 1513; mariners’ charts soon read “Dry Tortugas,” because the islands offered no fresh water. Wind, waves and storms keep reshaping them, and hurricanes have made a few of the smaller keys disappear and reappear. Between February and September as many as 100,000 sooty terns gather to nest on Bush Key, and green and loggerhead sea turtles nest on the beaches. [1] [1]

The keys sit beside the main shipping channel between the Gulf of Mexico, the western Caribbean and the Atlantic, and their reefs made the area one of the nation’s principal ship graveyards. On Garden Key, construction of Fort Jefferson began in 1846 and was never finished; the park brochure calls it the nation’s largest 1800s masonry fort. During the Civil War it served as a military prison, holding Union deserters and four men convicted of complicity in Lincoln’s assassination. Franklin D. Roosevelt proclaimed Fort Jefferson National Monument on January 4, 1935, and Congress redesignated it Dry Tortugas National Park on October 26, 1992, broadening its purpose to include the islands’ marine ecosystems. [1] [1]

black.html: How emancipation came to Fort Jefferson, the 2019 study says, was far from straightforward. In summer 1862 the fort’s commander, Col. Joseph S. Morgan, declared the enslaved workers at Forts Jefferson and Taylor “independent” of their owners; the Fort Taylor engineer protested. Because the Keys were under Union control, the study notes, the Emancipation Proclamation did not strictly apply there; Key West slaveholder James Filor wrote Lincoln seeking an exemption, arguing that U.S. government agents had induced Key West citizens to buy slaves for work on the forts, and failed. In 1863 the fort’s Black labor force became freedmen and women; the study found no known documentation of them specifically. From September 1865 to January 1866, companies of the 82nd U.S. Colored Infantry, organized in Louisiana in 1864, garrisoned the fort. [1] [1]

sources.title: Pirtle, Smith & Reed (New South Associates), The African American Experience at Fort Jefferson, 1847–1876, prepared for the NPS (2019)
Smith, Engineering Slavery: The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and Slavery at Key West, Florida Historical Quarterly 86(4), 2008

slavery.html: From 1847 to 1863 enslaved men leased by the Army Corps of Engineers, mostly from Key West, formed the core of Fort Jefferson’s labor force, alongside seasonal white workers, mostly Irish immigrants; enslaved women were brought to cook and do laundry. A 2019 study for the Park Service calls the practice industrial slavery and concludes that its use at Fort Jefferson and nearby Fort Taylor would solidify slavery’s hold on Key West. Historian Mark A. Smith (2008), assuming Fort Jefferson used a share similar to Fort Taylor’s roughly 9 percent, suggests that about 17 percent of Key West’s enslaved people worked for the engineers between 1845 and 1860. On July 10, 1847, seven men — Jerry Mason, Jack English, George English, John Thompson, and Ephraim, Howard and Robert Mallory — slipped away by night in four boats, bound for the Bahamas. They were brought back days later, and a guard was posted. [1] [1]

sources.title: Pirtle, Smith & Reed, The African American Experience at Fort Jefferson, 1847–1876 (NPS, 2019), ch. 2
Smith, Engineering Slavery, Florida Historical Quarterly 86(4), 2008, pp. 498–503

climate.html: The park’s 2017 foundation document records warmer ocean temperatures, increasing acidification of seawater, and coral bleaching and disease at the Dry Tortugas, and states that the associated effects of climate change have all been documented there. It lists sea-level rise and shoreline erosion as threats to island habitat and to turtle nesting beaches, rising temperatures as affecting sex ratios in sea turtles, and increasing storm intensity and frequency as a challenge to the ecosystem’s health and resilience. [1]
